title: Minimum wage and living wage: what is the difference?
author: Editorial Desk
summary: Two words that sound alike and mean different things.
body:
In debates about pay, two terms are used as if they meant the same thing: the minimum wage and the living wage. They do not. The difference between them explains why a worker can be paid exactly what the law requires and still struggle to feed a family, and it explains why unions keep asking for revision even after a wage has been legally notified. This post sets out the concepts, how India has fixed minimum wages over the years, what the new Code on Wages changes, and where the arguments now stand.

## The legal floor: the minimum wage

The minimum wage is the lowest wage that an employer may lawfully pay. In India it is fixed by the Central Government or by State Governments, for different industries, regions and levels of skill. The Minimum Wages Act, 1948, came into force on 15 March 1948, after earlier study by the Labour Investigation Committee in 1943 and a recommendation by the Standing Labour Committee in 1946 for a law to protect workers in poorly organised, low-paid employments. The Act was meant for workers who had little bargaining power and could be pressed into "sweated" conditions.

Three features of the minimum wage are worth stating plainly. Once fixed, it must be paid whatever the employer's capacity to pay. It is the same for men and women. And it is reviewed: under the Act, rates were to be revised at least every five years, and dearness allowance linked to a consumer price index is treated as part of the minimum wage in many cases and is revised twice a year. The Act did not itself define a minimum wage or give a formula for it. Those came from tripartite agreement and from the courts.

## Three levels of wage

The Committee on Fair Wages of 1948 described three levels. At the bottom is the minimum wage, which covers bare subsistence. At the top is the living wage, which allows a decent standard of life. Between the two lies the fair wage, which depends on the capacity of the industry to pay and on what comparable workers earn. The idea is that the minimum wage is a legal duty, the living wage is the goal, and the fair wage is the range that negotiation and industry conditions should settle.

## The need-based minimum wage of 1957

At the 15th Indian Labour Conference in 1957, representatives of Government, employers and workers agreed norms that are still widely used. They are worth listing because they show how detailed the thinking was:

- A standard working-class family is taken to have three consumption units per earner, and the earnings of women, children and adolescents are not counted.
- Food should supply 2,700 calories a day for an average adult of moderate activity.
- Clothing should be 72 yards per year for the family, taken as 18 yards per person.
- Rent should be at least the minimum rent charged under the Government's subsidised industrial housing scheme for low-income groups.
- Fuel, lighting and other miscellaneous items should be 20 per cent of the total minimum wage.

These norms were meant to convert the idea of "need" into numbers.

## The Reptakos Brett addition

In a case reported in 1992, the Supreme Court dealt with the claim of the workers of Reptakos Brett and Company and held that a further 25 per cent should be added to the wage to cover the needs not included in the 1957 norms: children's education, medical needs, minimum recreation including festivals, provision for old age and marriage. Together, the 1957 norms and the Reptakos addition give the six criteria that governments are expected to consider when they fix or revise minimum wages. In plain words, the law recognises that a family needs more than food, cloth and a roof.

## The national floor wage

A "national floor level minimum wage" was introduced in 1996, at Rs 35 a day, as a non-statutory benchmark that States were encouraged not to go below. It was revised from time to time using a consumer price index for industrial workers and reached Rs 176 a day in 2017. Because it had no legal force, States were encouraged but not obliged to follow it.

The Code on Wages changes this in a significant way. Under the Code, the Central Government fixes a floor wage on the basis of the standard of living of workers, and it may set different floor wages for different geographical areas. Minimum wages notified by the Centre or the States must be above the floor wage, and an existing minimum wage that is higher than the floor cannot be reduced. The Government's announcement of 21 November 2025, when the Codes came into force, said that minimum wages now apply to all workers, not only to those in a list of scheduled employments, and that wages must be paid on time. The Code also keeps the five-year review, allows the skill of the worker and the difficulty of the work to be considered, provides overtime at twice the normal rate, and says that deductions from wages cannot exceed 50 per cent of total wages.

## Where the gap lies

The distance between the legal minimum and a living wage is where most of the argument takes place. The 1957 norms and the Reptakos addition were framed decades ago, and unions argue that the wage notified in many places does not reflect the cost of rent, transport, medical care and schooling today. They also point out that notified wages are one thing and wages actually paid are another. A minimum wage that is not enforced, or that is paid in a different form from what is recorded, protects no one. Employers, for their part, point to the capacity of small enterprises to pay and to the risk that a high floor will push work into the informal economy. Both concerns are real, which is why the law talks of regular review and tripartite consultation and not of a single fixed number.

## What unions, including BMS, say

Unions, BMS among them, argue that actual minimum wages in many States fall short of these norms, and they ask for regular revision linked to price indices. They see the national floor wage under the Code as a possible base on which such revision can rest, provided the floor is set at a level that reflects need and is revised regularly. BMS has also tied the wage question to other demands in its memorandum to the Labour Minister, such as raising the wage ceilings for EPF and ESI and the ceiling for bonus calculation, since a ceiling that is not revised excludes workers who earn slightly more than the limit.

## What a worker can do

- Find out the notified minimum wage for the industry, skill category and area. It is published by the relevant government.
- Compare it with the wage slip, including dearness allowance.
- Keep records of days worked and hours, including overtime.
- Raise a written complaint with the labour authorities if wages fall short; the Code speaks of inspectors as facilitators first, but a complaint creates a record.

## A closing thought

A wage is not only a number. It is the arithmetic of a family's month: rent, food, a child's school fees, a visit to the doctor and something put aside for old age. The minimum wage ensures that the arithmetic does not fall below a certain line. The living wage describes where it should be. The task of the coming years is to move the first steadily towards the second, with honest records, regular revision and a floor that is more than a figure on paper.
